Interviewer:	I’ll tell you a little bit about the project to begin with and the questions I’ll be asking. Well, basically I’m looking at how the industrial placement year affects your career decisions and whether you still want to be an engineer and we’re trying to look at ways that we can get women to stay in engineering long-term.

Subject:	OK.

Interviewer:	Can you just remind me what course you’re doing?

Subject:	Mechanical engineering.

Interviewer:	Right, OK and what A levels did you do?

Subject:	Er, physics, chemistry, with AS level Maths and Theatre Studies.

Interviewer:	Ok, how old are you?

Subject:	19.

Interviewer:	19 – did you come straight from doing A levels to university then?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	What type of school did you go to?

Subject:	Girl’s Grammar School.

Interviewer:	Right and have you got any previous work experience?

Subject:	Er, I did a Nuffield bursary for 4 weeks with [company 1] and last time I worked with [company 2].

Interviewer:	Right, OK – what do your parents do?

Subject:	Er my mother’s a nurse and my dad is a self-support engineer.

Interviewer:	OK, I’m just going to ask you now, a few things about how you decided to go into engineering really. So, when and why did you decide to enter engineering?

Subject:	Erm, I was always interested in Maths and Physics and I did my – how theoretical physics was – so I started looking into engineering (OK) see if that was suited better.

Interviewer:	OK, what factors do you think influenced your decision – like family and education and your strengths? Like why did you decide to do the Maths and Physics and maybe not Sociology or something like that?

Subject:	Erm, I’ve always been very practical. I mean I can guild numbers – anything with key words, or trying to fill up 2 sides of A4 when it only needs half a side, to be precise (Mm) I’ve just never been able to do. And it’s the same kind of thing – both of my parents are the same way, but yeah.

Interviewer:	OK. Did you know any engineers to talk to? Did you say your dad was an engineer?

Subject:	Erm, he’s sales support – he’s – he doesn’t – he’s not an engineer he just runs the technical side of the sales, proves that it’s not illegal (yeah) or dangerous to build it. He doesn’t do any actual engineering.

Interviewer:	He’s just in the industry?

Subject:	Yeah, he used to be an apprentice, he did an apprenticeship with [company]Forecast to be an engineer, but it closed down – he stopped doing that.

Interviewer:	OK, what kind of things appeal to you about engineering? Is it the practical?

Subject:	The practical side and being able to see something – even design something – you’re likely to see it come out the end (yeah) or be able to go and run a test and see the final result, and see it go out to manufacture. (Yeah) It just brings the whole process really of being able to do things – different parts of the process, rather than being stuck doing one or the other. You can see so much further.

Interviewer:	Yes, so it’s quite a satisfying feeling – project – see it all.

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, what was it that specifically attracted you to mechanical engineering? Was there a reason that you didn’t want to study say Civil engineering?

Subject:	Erm, I hadn’t ever really considered doing civil and things like that, because it never really got talked about. When I was looking into engineering it was more aero or auto mechanical systems. Those were the only ones that got talked about and I didn’t want to specify – as much to do – just aero or auto. And, er, mechanical was just – it was varied enough for you to get as much out of it as you wanted to, regarding – to varying a module and everything and not knowing much about it, within the (?) of doing it. So it seemed a better choice.

Interviewer:	What sort of research did you do? You said that civil and that weren’t really talked about it (lost words)?

Subject:	It was things like erm, the careers officer at school, the insight courses I went on – it was never really, they just went, and if they did do things outside those four it was normally chemical engineering, and all the materials engineering and then things like that.

Interviewer:	Have your family been supportive of your choices?

Subject:	Er my Dad was, my mum wasn’t.

Interviewer:	She wanted you to do something else?

Subject:	She thought I should be doing Maths or Accounting, because she thought there was better job prospects and the course wouldn’t be as heavy, so I’d find it easier.

Interviewer:	Was it difficult for you with her not supporting you?

Subject:	Well, not so much now, it was in the first year, because if I had any problems or if – there were some weeks all the coursework was due in, I was having a panic, it became I told you not to do the course and things like that, which was a bit hard but now she’s kind of accepted the fact I’m here whether she likes it or not.

Interviewer:	OK, you say you went to Careers people (yeah) were they supportive?

Subject:	Er, yeah. Our school was, at the time, trying to go for a Beacon school in Science and things like that and I kind of became their token engineer for the year – because they kind of said, because they always tried to get and have – well always ended up having an engineer, a doctor and I can’t remember what the other one is –but either way it’s kind– that kind of thing, so when they thought I might be interested in doing it (yeah) they backed me up a lot for it, so …

Interviewer:	Did you feel a bit like they pushed you too much sometimes or didn’t you mind that?

Subject:	No, I quite liked it because a lot of the other people who were trying to find out about what they wanted to do, were having a lot of trouble getting hold of information and things, although I was kind of given all the help I wanted to because the Careers people were really into it, my Physics teacher was really excited about it and things like that.

Interviewer:	OK, are you going on a placement?

Subject:	Hopefully, I haven’t had any responses yet.

Interviewer:	Right, OK. What do you think it was that made you want to do a Sandwich course?

Subject:	Erm, well firstly because 4 week – 4 years, straight through University seemed like a lot to take on really (yes) because I’ve always wanted to do things like placement stuff, even if it was just to see which bits of engineering I didn’t want to do. (Yeah) So, it’s kind of knowing where I want to go when I’m finished. Gain the experience and just seeing how it does work in the real world, as opposed to design this and you have a lathe and this. And knowing what’s out there.

Interviewer:	OK. How did you decide to come to [this] University?

Subject:	Erm, it was mainly through erm league tables and things because it kept coming up as something I should look at, and erm, yeah, when I came to apply it was looking for the right grades, so I signed up.

Interviewer:	OK. When you decided that you were interested in engineering did you realise that it was so male dominated?

Subject:	Yeah, but I’ve never really seen that as a problem. (OK) It’s one of these things that people keep quoting to me and trying – well you both doing your job – as long as they do their job and get on with it. I’m not bothered, at all.

Interviewer:	Do you think that more women should be encouraged into engineering?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know. Most of the girls I knew and grew up with, and like I’m meeting now (yeah) they wouldn’t fit in with it. They don’t tend to like – they aren’t people who have done physics stuff, - the people who are more into things like computing and stuff like that. It would be a nice idea but I don’t think many people – it’s not just that they aren’t being aware of it, as an option, they don’t really want to be doing it and – because they’re kind of happy with the idea of doing design and things, it’s just the idea that comes with it, of having to put on overalls and fiddle with the stuff. And they just don’t see it as something they’d like to do, the same way that a lot of the blokes I know wouldn’t go into it because they don’t like that kind of thing. 

Interviewer:	Do you think that the reason people might think they don’t want to do it is based on true ideas or false perceptions about what it is really like?

Subject:	I think they’re partially true ideas because – but they can get overtaken a lot. Sometimes people do see it as getting down, getting something, stripping it apart or rebuilding it. And they kind of miss the fact that its not just that, you’re doing – like on the chemicals you’re doing fluids and you’re doing design work and all the rest of things. 99% of the time you’re behind a computer and like one module every year, I think, is actually taking stuff apart, so…

Interviewer:	OK, what characteristics do you think makes a good engineer? If you had to describe an ideal engineer?

Subject:	Er, don’t know – analytical, needing to find out how things work – just curious about everything, I think, just so that you know you can design something, you know, look at it and actually go no I can make it better or – why not do this instead and all the rest of it.

Interviewer:	And you said earlier that you didn’t think it mattered whether you’re a male or a female, but do you think that there are any advantages or disadvantages to being a woman engineer?

Subject:	Erm, not really. Erm, but then again some people, you know, on placements were saying that because there aren’t enough women engineers, people are more likely to give us jobs. And a lot of the blokes are – and it’s a bit annoying but it is true in some cases, because I know that my [company 2] placement was because it was a female engineer.

Interviewer:	Like positive discrimination?

Subject:	Yeah, but then again it’s also – it can work the other way, so I think overall it works out – it’s just a bit unfortunate that people still see it like that (yeah) for it to work in the first place.

Interviewer:	OK, let’s talk a bit about your course and your experiences on the course so far. What did you expect from your degree, in terms of like the skills that you’ve learnt and maybe the gender proportions and the type of teaching and things like that?

Subject:	Er, gender proportions I was quite surprised how few girls there were, on a course of 140, because I think there’s maybe 10/15 us possibly in our year, er which was a bit of a surprise at how low it was – ‘cos I knew it was low. I don’t know – the course itself is – I don’t know, I expected the course to be more intense than it was, kind of, because it’s always been built up as this really hard course which nobody wants to do, and all the rest of it, and it’s a lot of work. But, it’s what I thought, but it’s not as time consuming as I thought (yeah) because it’s a lot of in lectures stuff, rather than a lot of courses 6 hours, but then you’ve got to do 3 weeks worth of reading for next week and things like that.

Interviewer:	OK what do you think have been the best and worst things about the course so far?

Subject:	Erm, the worst thing is the group projects possibly, because we don’t get enough information to do a lot of the stuff, so we’re always getting cross (?) because they’re usually run by more than one of the lecturers. So it’s very confusing and your – your goals aren’t set (yeah) and then when people start getting irritated and it doesn’t work well. The best bit is I’m finally understanding a lot of stuff, because last year was a lot of learning new things and now it’s generally more or less apply what you’ve learnt last year and I can (so its all starting to make sense?) yeah its all starting coming together and we’re looking at more interesting things rather than basic examples.

Interviewer:	OK, have you been taught by male and female lecturers?

Subject:	We’ve had one female lecturer so far and she wasn’t very good (laughs). Erm, no there’s been a general consensus on our course that the one female lecturer we’ve had is possible the worst role model we could’ve ever asked for and we prefer – we much prefer just having whoever.

Interviewer:	Yeah, do you think that was anything to do with her being a woman or just she wasn’t a very good lecturer?

Subject:	I think she was just an appalling lecturer rather than being a woman, but it was – I think she got away with doing some of the things she did because she was – at times she was a female employee and she was pregnant. (Right) Because there were a lot of complaints made and I think nothing has happened about it.

Interviewer:	OK, and can you give any examples of where she wasn’t as good compared to others who work here – lecturers?

Subject:	Er, she lost respect mainly from the first lecture, because she came in 10 minutes late and then spent another 10 minutes trying to set up, and was very moody and the lecture hadn’t started so we were talking – I think we were still talking mainly about the last lecture, and she just turned round and shouted at everyone about not being able to hear herself think. As soon as she started the lecture we shut up straight away. She then had another go at the class about finally we were actually able to be quiet, her notes – 52 pages of notes on the first lecture for – it was meant to be for the whole course but there were so many mistakes in it and they were somebody else’s notes she’d edited. So everyone just lost patience with her – completely.

Interviewer:	And nothing, despite all your efforts, was done about it?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	OK, do you have a personal tutor?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Are they male or female?

Subject:	Male.

Interviewer:	Have you been to them or are they approachable if you needed to go to them?

Subject:	They’re approachable erm yeah – Colin’s quite good.

Interviewer:	Are you happy with him being a male personal tutor or would you rather have had a female?

Subject:	I don’t think it makes much difference because the kind of problems that I’d go to my personal tutor with aren’t – they’re not of a sensitive nature or anything, so…

Interviewer:	OK, who or what do you think has been the greatest influence on you, since you started your degree?

Subject:	Erm, that’s a big one (it’s OK) I’ve no idea (that’s OK)

Interviewer:	You said earlier that you’ve had some problems with group work. (yes) Has the type of teaching that you’ve had involved quite a lot of groupwork?

Subject:	There’s 2 or 3 yes, so it’s not too much, but they tend to be things like double modules and things (yeah) – so they count for a lot but it’s a not a lot of actual work in the group.

Interviewer:	When you work in groups do you get to choose yourself who you work with or are you put into groups?

Subject:	Er, half the time you get to choose and half the time you get put in groups. For lab work and things, most of the time we’re given the option, we’ll be put into groups, but if you want someone particularly in the group – if you email them they’ll arrange it, so.

Interviewer:	How do you decide who to work with in those situations?

Subject:	Erm, normally I don’t pick who I work with, I just erm wait till everyone else has been put in the group and work with somebody new because I’d rather work with as many people as possible, even if it’s just so that when there is a point where I am put in a group with someone – I know how much I can trust them to get things done. (OK) If we’ve got to pick groups, it’s generally people I’ve worked with before, or people I get on fairly well with.

Interviewer:	Have you had any particular good or bad experiences of working in groups?

Subject:	Er, recently we had a meeting for a CAD MAC project. The day before it was due in to finish off, out of 4 of us, only 2 turned up – 1 of them sent an email telling us it was – that the coursework wasn’t due until the week after, so he wasn’t going to meet until next week. Erm, which arrived after getting an email saying that we were definitely handing it in this week. But that’s kind of the worst one so far – well, other than working with my house mate but that’s just a bad idea, it was more my own fault, so…

Interviewer:	Ok, do you think that men or women are better to work with or is it…?

Subject:	Not really mixed groups tend to be the best – well I find – well because if there are a couple of guys on the course who – where they’ve actually done – specially design and make projects, where they’ve actually done some machining or things, they tend to try to take over. And if you’ve got a mixed group, usually you can get some back up for everything you’re going to say. Even if it’s just quieting everyone down so they’ll actually listen. Er, it’s also because we do actually look at things a slightly different way, and it just brings up a few more alternatives (yeah) to look at, and things to take into account.

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s maybe another advantage of having female engineers, that they bring a different perspective?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	What aspects of university teaching or advice, do you think will help you on your placement if you go?

Subject:	I don’t know, ‘cos I’ve managed to avoid applying for anything which has to go through the placement officer

Interviewer:	Is there a particular reason for that?

Subject:	I don’t like the idea of it being put through – that these are [university] students – they are meant to be the best and being put in for companies who always take in [university] students, which seem to be what most of those ones are. I’d rather have sent in my CV, covering letter or do the on-line thing, and just say, this is me, this is what I’ve done, do you want to employ me or not?

Interviewer:	So they’re taking you because you are a [university] student. OK, what skills from the course do you think that you’ll take to a placement with you?

Subject:	I think a lot of the CAD design work will go with me because up until university I hated doing any design work (yeah) whatsoever and just because of the sheer volume of it, we’ve had to do and things, erm, I’ve got used to it and I kind of know how the process works in industry from things like [company 2] and stuff.

Interviewer:	Yeah, do you think those work experiences will help you on your placement as well?

Subject:	Yeah, just ‘cos it gives me an idea of company culture and the way things work – kind of where it comes at this point, this department works and then this department (?) comes to there – we do this and all the rest of it so, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, do you feel prepared and ready to go on placement?

Subject:	Erm, mostly. I’m still a bit worried about not knowing enough, especially because I don’t know exactly where I’m going or what I’ll be expected to do at that company.

Interviewer:	Yeah, what sort of companies have you been applying to?

Subject:	Everything from er [company] to [company], erm [organisation] – anything which sounds like it could be more than just being sat at an office doing one thing time and time again, so…

Interviewer:	So the criteria that you’ve set when you’re looking for companies have been quite broad?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	OK do you think that your educational experience, or the way that you’re taught, reflects the realities of what it’ll be like when you’re working in the industry?

Subject:	Er, yes, especially the 2nd year because the 1st year was all – because it was just, you need to learn this (yeah) and now the lecturers are a lot more, well, you just look it up because if you’re working, you just find this handbook and go there and you do it like this and sort of – they aren’t so heavily into things like deriving certain formulas and things – well, you know this, so you can just do this or you’ve made this assumption, you can do that or you don’t need to worry about making it exact. If it passes that then do an exact point, so it’s much more realistic than being sat down and told the exact way you need to do x, y and z.

Interviewer:	Do you think the group work will help you in terms of not say the technical skills, but interacting with other people as well? Do you think that bit’s useful?

Subject:	Yes, just to know what it’s like to be working with new people and different people and even when it does go wrong, how to, kind of deal with it – and get the project done instead of sitting, complaining about it and causing problems.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the placement idea, in general, is a good idea and that students should be encouraged to go on placements?

Subject:	Yes, because if nothing else, 4 years is a very long time and because you don’t do like engineering A level, or whatever, it is a good time to go and look at the industry and sort of – like, you might turn round and say, well actually no, this isn’t what I need to be doing. And instead of, like wasting another 2 years doing something you really hate and can see like nothing else in the future, you can turn around and try to do something else or think of something new.

Interviewer:	OK, do you know anyone on your course that isn’t going, or doesn’t want to go on placement?

Subject:	Er, yeah but most of them are either doing a BEng and kind of have a job waiting for them when they go out or they’ve already taken gap years and don’t want to be, like, 26 when they graduate or whatever, so they just want to sort it out. But then again most of them are planning to go on the graduate development where they do 2 years of more or less a placement before you start work and things like that.

Interviewer:	OK, has anyone tried to really encourage you or discourage you from going on a placement?

Subject:	Erm, not really – occasionally you get a few comments about just doing the 4 years to get it finished and then go and earn money, but nothing really serious.

Interviewer:	And what about comments from friends and family or…?

Subject:	Friends of the family – I think people who are already in electrical engineering or things like that and they don’t see the point – it’s just wasting a year. Its their opinion and their entitled to it.

Interviewer:	Yeah, you said you have applied for the placements off your own back (yeah) have the university supported you doing that…?

Subject:	Well, a lot of them came off a list we were given. They said these people will take placements, which came off a list. Not a lot of placements on the list were actually, you must apply through the university, so it’s not too bad. I don’t think the university mind as long as you end up somewhere, or decide what you’re doing, because in the long run, it’s your placement, you can go where you want.

Interviewer:	But have the university been supportive, if you do need to go to them for help and (Yeah) in finding stuff. The type of companies that you’ve been applying to - is there anything that particularly attracted you to them or have you been completely open minded, or are you thinking …

Subject:	I’ve been completely open minded, yeah but I’m most interested in looking at things which look at research rather than design work, or where I can go out on site for a bit and come back, and things like that.

Interviewer:	Have you, when you’ve been considering organisations, looked at things other than the type of work they do, have you looked at things like training opportunities, and pay and equal opportunities, or anything like that, or…?

Subject:	Er, I’ve looked a bit at the training but most companies I’ve looked at er things like the [company], [company], have the training programmes in place and they mention that well, if you do this we might sort of take you on afterwards (yeah), and put you on graduate development, and things like that – which is a bonus but I’m not going to go and apply to someone I’m not particularly keen on so that I can get extra training.

Interviewer:	Yeah, OK. How long have you got to wait to find out?

Subject:	Er, when the companies decide to tell me and we’ve been told that people still advertise placements up to June (oh right) and in some cases people aren’t giving placements until like the October. So I think its generally up to you, when you put a cut off point on when you came to – you turn round and just say well, you’re not getting a placement now, I’d just carry on (yeah) or take a year out – see what happens.

Interviewer:	Yeah, OK. Did you start off with the list that the University gave you and then where did you do from there? Did you go and look at their web sites?

Subject:	Go and look at web sites or email them, asking them for material on it and stuff. 

Interviewer:	And have you had to have any interviews?

Subject:	Erm, just the one with [company] at the moment.

Interviewer:	OK, what type of things are you expecting to get out of your placement?

Subject:	Well, just knowing where I want to be heading when I finish here – kind of an idea of how industry works instead of the classroom kind of environment so…

Interviewer:	Kind of putting the theory into practice (yeah). OK, do you think that it will improve your career prospects at the end being able to say that you have been on a placement?

Subject:	Yeah, ‘cos it shows that you have got some idea of erm being grounded in industry rather than saying I know all this theory like everyone else does. You can apply it, knowing what’s needed for what and…

Interviewer:	What do you think could be the worst and the best things about being on a placement?

Subject:	Er, the best thing will be meeting – making new contacts (yeah) because a lot of the companies will help you – like find me a project and things and helping you out with information. The worst is probably moving to wherever the placement is and being somewhere completely new and having to live with total strangers (yeah) for a whole year where you can’t just turn round and then say no, I’m not going to have this any more.

Interviewer:	Have you applied to organisations over quite a wide geography then?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	OK. What are you most looking forward to?

Subject:	Erm, being back in the real world – if that doesn’t sound really strange but [university town] is just [university town] because there’s so many students here, I don’t really hear the outside world too much, it’s [this university’s] done this, or [this university’s] done that – it’s just being out there and being, you know, being normal again – going to work, earning money, working regular time and going out and doing what you want at the weekends and coming back.

Interviewer:	What type of work do you hope to be doing?

Subject:	Research, hopefully.

Interviewer:	Yeah.

Subject:	And defence would be an ideal but erm such high standards are required for it, I’d be lucky to get in there.

Interviewer:	OK, how do you expect work to differ from university?

Subject:	Er, much more scheduled and much more your own responsibility and therefore, you need to plan for this week and this for next week – being given an end point to aim for and to do it yourself – just being able to do 9 till 5 and then anything else is what you want to do – what you need to do because you haven’t done it during your day role, and random hours and having to fill most of them, if you haven’t quite sorted yourself out.

Interviewer:	And are you looking forward to that side of it?

Subject:	Yeah, er much more structured routine would just be nice for a change – instead of random hours, just knowing what’s happening.

Interviewer:	OK, in terms of your career, where do you see yourself in 2 years time?

Subject:	In 2 years time, erm, I’ll be in my 3rd – just to finish my 3rd year and to go into my 4th year – (?) I won’t really be…

Interviewer:	Alright, what about in 5 years?

Subject:	Er, hopefully, I’ll have just finished the graduate development programme – somewhere – and be looking at erm getting myself in whatever area I’ve found useful during the programme (uh huh) and starting work for real.

Interviewer:	Yeah, what about in 10 years time?

Subject:	Hopefully I will have got my chartership (yeah) and still working for the same company – possibly.

Interviewer:	OK, what would be your ideal career?

Subject:	Er, my ideal would be working for someone like [company] on [place] because they have the funding, with being linked to the MoD and there erm defence, but when they became a public company did a lot more alternative work as well now – freelance work – so you wouldn’t ever be – you’d still have the main defence work which has a huge amount of innovation, most of the time, but you’d still be able to come out of that and still do something much more down to earth or new and interesting. It’s just – split it up so I didn’t I end up being one of these people like er at [company 2], where they just know everything about the one product, but if you try and talk to them about something else, it always comes back to focussing on the stair lift and it becomes very closed as to how you look at things.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that you will come across many difficulties trying to get that ideal career? Do you think it’s realistic?

Subject:	I think it’s possible erm, they’re still trying to recruit a lot more people at the moment. As long as my grades stay up, I’m in for a chance – everyone’s in for a chance.

Interviewer:	Yeah, so the main thing between you and that, you think is, academic?

Subject:	Is grades, if I can. Well Kinetic is – it’s kind of local to where I’m from – it’s where the – if you had someone from engineering come into schools – it’d be someone who’s from the MoD, and then it became Kinetic and things like that, so I’ve always had a link with them. (Yeah) So, I think if I can get the grades, I want to work there to the point where, hopefully, if I manage to get to an interview, I’ll be able to put it across that even if I’m borderline on academics and experience, I’ve got enough enthusiasm and determination to want to work with them – that it’ll be enough to get me the job.

Interviewer:	OK, have you applied to them for a placement?

Subject:	No because they’ve stopped doing placements this year. They’ve started doing sponsorship programme instead (OK) which you can’t apply to once you’re at university.

Interviewer:	OK, and would you have been interested in doing the sponsorship at the time?

Subject:	I was, but I didn’t see companies I knew much about and I was a bit dubious about signing up for, and taking money off them to be doing a summer placement every year – a year out with them and turning out that actually, no ...

Interviewer:	Yeah, what if you didn’t actually want it …

Subject:	If [company] had been offering one then I’d have probably gone for it (yeah) because I knew about them, same for a couple of others, but at the time it didn’t seem applicable.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that career prospects are good in your field of engineering?

Subject:	Yeah, because they can’t – the quotas at the moment, for graduates in mechanical engineering aren’t that good, they’re just trying to get more people in and it’s – on my course a lot of the people who are there are on – didn’t apply for mechanical engineering, they’re people who tried for auto or aero and didn’t make the grades, and considering some of the grades required, if you wanted to get onto the course – first time – the fact that there’s still loads of clearing places and they’re able to put as many people on there as wanted, just shows that they really do need to have a lot more graduates with a degree, than we’re getting.

Interviewer:	What about the prospects once you’re inside a company for going into say the managing side of it, would you be interested in doing that?

Subject:	I would prefer to stay with research but a lot of people I’ve talked to in companies, its more or less, if you have a degree, you can get almost straight into managerial positions if you want to but I personally find – hold off doing that until I’ve had at least 2/3 years working almost at ground level and learning that – ‘cos I don’t think it’s right to go – to manage a thing when you have no idea about how it works and when you’ve only just got into grips with the company and things like that.

Interviewer:	OK. And are you happy with the career choices that you’ve made so far?

Subject:	Er, yeah.

Interviewer:	Would you do anything differently if you had to do it all again?

Subject:	Erm, yes, possibly talk to a few more people who had done engineering, just to make myself slightly more aware of the workload and what to expect. (yeah) But, apart from that, no.

Interviewer:	OK, how would you describe the culture or the characteristics of the engineering industry in 5 words?

Subject:	Er, rooted in old ways (traditional) yeah, you can see the same kind of patterns everywhere, it doesn’t change much even when new productions methods or new things – it kind of alters a little bit and then it goes back into the same old patterns. Its well established – it doesn’t – it takes quite a bit to do a shake up, completely.

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s maybe the reason why there don’t seem to be more women going into engineering – whereas they maybe doing in other fields?

Subject:	Erm, possibly. I think it’s more this image of the boiler suits and things and then looking at sort of the money and things, because for the same A level courses, if you did computing - I mean its even obvious with my house mate who’s doing a placement next year in computing – she’s getting 17 ½ grand for her placement year (blimey) – whereas I’m looking at 12. So it’s kind of looking at career choices and first impressions of it, because if you don’t think you’re going to be doing as well, you won’t look into it further to see sort of what you can do.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the engineering culture is masculine?

Subject:	Er, fairly but just because it always has been and how it started off, was very much sort of, most companies was a guy who built something and then it became a company so everyone – and a lot of people – the companies I’ve worked in, have started off doing things, like apprenticeships rather than degrees, so they have worked on the shop floor, and they do know everything about it and they can like strip down whatever they’re building and build it back up in like 2 seconds. And I’ve been to some companies – 30 years they’ve been going – as an under grad going, I’d do it like this, and they’re like, well no, and they can just see everything – and it does give you the perception that everything is really hands-on (yeah) whereas you stay there for a few weeks and you actually realise that no, they haven’t done that in like 30 years – so, it’s just the way they’ve started bringing people in.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that if more women do go into the industry, that will break those perceptions down?

Subject:	I think it’ll start to, especially as they start getting higher up, because then they’ll be like role models. It’s like engineering – you’ve got [university] and people like that, and its like, the guy who did railways and bridges and big heavy things like – they’re either like – the only vaguely engineering woman, I think she’s – I can’t think of her name – she’s a materials engineer and she’s done a lot of work on polymers and stuff, so she’s a Royal Fellow now, but that’s the only the one I’ve heard of and that’s only because I read things like New Scientist and that lot, so haven’t kind of been pointed to, oh look this woman managed to do it and all the rest of it.

Interviewer:	Do you think that role models are important then (yeah) to encourage people?

Subject:	Well with big role models, because – I mean, with WES here, it’s like they occasionally get someone in to talk and it’s like, oh she is a manager of a project for – oh it’s sort of, yes, she has a job, she has the same kind of managerial role as anyone else who’d have it and it’s not really that inspiring – like you’ll end up in that job rather than you’d be famous for it, you know, and it’s like, computers have their people to look at and sort of biologists and engineering is just kind of a few big men at the top and you don’t know much else at all.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think any aspects of the engineering culture will be problematic for you?

Subject:	Not really but then again I work with people – when I worked for [company 2] and things they were really accommodating about it, and they were very aware of the fact that they need a lot more women. A lot of them were much more receptive to we need more people and if it comes in the form of women – we don’t care. We just need to get the fresh in-takes coming in, so I don’t think it’ll be too big a problem. It’ll just be maybe, some people who’ve been there a long time and aren’t used to it, being a bit strange, but I mean that’s getting used to anything. You could say if you suddenly gave me a new computer system, they’d be a bit odd. But I don’t think it’s anything that’s like directly related to suddenly having a woman in the workplace.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think your educational experience is different from other students, say in social sciences?

Subject:	Er, I don’t know – more because – because of the A levels I did, I’ve always been associated with people who’ve done similar courses so I don’t really know enough people who’ve done – the none sciences – to gauge if it’s that much different, if you know what I mean.

Interviewer:	OK, you mentioned WES, have you been in that group since you started university?

Subject:	I’ve been a member since I was 16 (right) with outside groups and doing their insight course. Last year I was a member here and was part of one their projects. Technically, I’m a member now but I haven’t been involved in it, after last year because it was - I couldn’t see much reason for some of the things they were doing (right, OK) so it didn’t seem like it was worth it when I could be concentrating on other things.

Interviewer:	What sorts of things were they involved in?

Subject:	Well a lot of it is getting women in from the industry as – like a role model, like a [company] production line manager which, having someone talk about their job as a production line manager, especially having worked for a bit in production, with [company 2], I’d much rather go out and try and get myself experience – you’re writing to companies – than to be sitting, having someone telling me I’ve become a Chartered Engineer, it’s great, you can do it too, because if I didn’t think I could do it, I wouldn’t be here – yeah, and there’s just – they run other projects, which sound really worthwhile trying to get kids into engineering, especially girls, erm last year it was an email mentoring but people they’re targeting aren’t organised enough for it to work. I ended up mentoring a girl who just didn’t do any emails – didn’t want to know. She’d been put in there because the school said she was in the A set at maths, therefore she should want to do things like engineering. She didn’t. She wanted to be a biologist, which I know nothing about, so even if she had emailed me about what she wanted to do, I couldn’t have helped her. It’s just badly organised. I mean some things this year, are things like lego competition, which is a national thing and they were just helping out with – are really good causes and I’d love to do it but I don’t have the time to do it and I don’t have the inclination to take out the 3 hours.

Interviewer:	Do you think there’s anything different that they should be doing that they’re maybe not doing?

Subject:	Erm, I think because this is a student group erm it’s being more aimed at trying to get people into the uni, than getting people outside to do better, or to get companies who already work with the uni to go oh, we’re great. Erm, ‘cos a lot of the other groups are doing things like we’ve managed to get a trip to so and so’s factory. They’re going to give us a tour, show us how it all works, so if you’re interested come to that. They’re running conferences in the centres and things, which sounds really interesting if I could get – but they’re not accessible from here.

Interviewer:	Yeah, do you think that the mentoring idea is a good idea in general? Not just say you being a mentor, but would you like to have a mentor as you went into the industry?

Subject:	Yeah – I mean at A level, we had various mentors and things and it’s always just given me someone to bounce off ideas with or to just check that even if it’s like, just a random person, but it’s one of these things I think you’ve got to want to do and your mentor’s got to want to do because if you can’t be bothered or just don’t want to know, you know, and then you don’t want to do it and it’s just like oh, I won’t bother then. As long as both people involved are active for it – up for it, I think it’s a great scheme, but it’s a case of choosing who’s involved with what.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s everything thank you very much.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what factors do you think influenced your decision – like family and education and your strengths? Like why did you decide to do the Maths and Physics and maybe not Sociology or something like that?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Did you know any engineers to talk to? Did you say your dad was an engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.text: He’s just in the industry?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what kind of things appeal to you about engineering? Is it the practical?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The practical side and being able to see something – even design something – you’re likely to see it come out the end (yeah) or be able to go and run a test and see the final result, and see it go out to manufacture. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, so it’s quite a satisfying feeling – project – see it all.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what was it that specifically attracted you to mechanical engineering? Was there a reason that you didn’t want to study say Civil engineering?

So it seemed a better choice.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What sort of research did you do? You said that civil and that weren’t really talked about it (lost words)?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It was things like erm, the careers officer at school, the insight courses I went on – it was never really, they just went, and if they did do things outside those four it was normally chemical engineering, and all the materials engineering and then things like that.

turns.text: Have your family been supportive of your choices?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er my Dad was, my mum wasn’t.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: She wanted you to do something else?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Was it difficult for you with her not supporting you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, not so much now, it was in the first year, because if I had any problems or if – there were some weeks all the coursework was due in, I was having a panic, it became I told you not to do the course and things like that, which was a bit hard but now she’s kind of accepted the fact I’m here whether she likes it or not.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, you say you went to Careers people (yeah) were they supportive?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yeah. Our school was, at the time, trying to go for a Beacon school in Science and things like that and I kind of became their token engineer for the year – because they kind of said, because they always tried to get and have – well always ended up having an engineer, a doctor and I can’t remember what the other one is –but either way it’s kind– that kind of thing, so when they thought I might be interested in doing it (yeah) they backed me up a lot for it, so …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you feel a bit like they pushed you too much sometimes or didn’t you mind that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I quite liked it because a lot of the other people who were trying to find out about what they wanted to do, were having a lot of trouble getting hold of information and things, although I was kind of given all the help I wanted to because the Careers people were really into it, my Physics teacher was really excited about it and things like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are you going on a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hopefully, I haven’t had any responses yet.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Right, OK. What do you think it was that made you want to do a Sandwich course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well firstly because 4 week – 4 years, straight through University seemed like a lot to take on really (yes) because I’ve always wanted to do things like placement stuff, even if it was just to see which bits of engineering I didn’t want to do. (Yeah) So, it’s kind of knowing where I want to go when I’m finished. Gain the experience and just seeing how it does work in the real world, as opposed to design this and you have a lathe and this. And knowing what’s out there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. How did you decide to come to [this] University?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, it was mainly through erm league tables and things because it kept coming up as something I should look at, and erm, yeah, when I came to apply it was looking for the right grades, so I signed up.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. When you decided that you were interested in engineering did you realise that it was so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, but I’ve never really seen that as a problem. (OK) It’s one of these things that people keep quoting to me and trying – well you both doing your job – as long as they do their job and get on with it. I’m not bothered, at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that more women should be encouraged into engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t know. Most of the girls I knew and grew up with, and like I’m meeting now (yeah) they wouldn’t fit in with it. They don’t tend to like – they aren’t people who have done physics stuff, - the people who are more into things like computing and stuff like that. It would be a nice idea but I don’t think many people – it’s not just that they aren’t being aware of it, as an option, they don’t really want to be doing it and – because they’re kind of happy with the idea of doing design and things, it’s just the idea that comes with it, of having to put on overalls and fiddle with the stuff. And they just don’t see it as something they’d like to do, the same way that a lot of the blokes I know wouldn’t go into it because they don’t like that kind of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the reason people might think they don’t want to do it is based on true ideas or false perceptions about what it is really like?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think they’re partially true ideas because – but they can get overtaken a lot. Sometimes people do see it as getting down, getting something, stripping it apart or rebuilding it. And they kind of miss the fact that its not just that, you’re doing – like on the chemicals you’re doing fluids and you’re doing design work and all the rest of things. 99% of the time you’re behind a computer and like one module every year, I think, is actually taking stuff apart, so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what characteristics do you think makes a good engineer? If you had to describe an ideal engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, don’t know – analytical, needing to find out how things work – just curious about everything, I think, just so that you know you can design something, you know, look at it and actually go no I can make it better or – why not do this instead and all the rest of it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And you said earlier that you didn’t think it mattered whether you’re a male or a female, but do you think that there are any advantages or disadvantages to being a woman engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, not really. Erm, but then again some people, you know, on placements were saying that because there aren’t enough women engineers, people are more likely to give us jobs. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Like positive discrimination?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, but then again it’s also – it can work the other way, so I think overall it works out – it’s just a bit unfortunate that people still see it like that (yeah) for it to work in the first place.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, let’s talk a bit about your course and your experiences on the course so far. What did you expect from your degree, in terms of like the skills that you’ve learnt and maybe the gender proportions and the type of teaching and things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, gender proportions I was quite surprised how few girls there were, on a course of 140, because I think there’s maybe 10/15 us possibly in our year, er which was a bit of a surprise at how low it was – ‘cos I knew it was low. I don’t know – the course itself is – I don’t know, I expected the course to be more intense than it was, kind of, because it’s always been built up as this really hard course which nobody wants to do, and all the rest of it, and it’s a lot of work. But, it’s what I thought, but it’s not as time consuming as I thought (yeah) because it’s a lot of in lectures stuff, rather than a lot of courses 6 hours, but then you’ve got to do 3 weeks worth of reading for next week and things like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK what do you think have been the best and worst things about the course so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, the worst thing is the group projects possibly, because we don’t get enough information to do a lot of the stuff, so we’re always getting cross (?) because they’re usually run by more than one of the lecturers. So it’s very confusing and your – your goals aren’t set (yeah) and then when people start getting irritated and it doesn’t work well. The best bit is I’m finally understanding a lot of stuff, because last year was a lot of learning new things and now it’s generally more or less apply what you’ve learnt last year and I can (so its all starting to make sense?) yeah its all starting coming together and we’re looking at more interesting things rather than basic examples.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you been taught by male and female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: We’ve had one female lecturer so far and she wasn’t very good (laughs). Erm, no there’s been a general consensus on our course that the one female lecturer we’ve had is possible the worst role model we could’ve ever asked for and we prefer – we much prefer just having whoever.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, do you think that was anything to do with her being a woman or just she wasn’t a very good lecturer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think she was just an appalling lecturer rather than being a woman, but it was – I think she got away with doing some of the things she did because she was – at times she was a female employee and she was pregnant. (Right) Because there were a lot of complaints made and I think nothing has happened about it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, and can you give any examples of where she wasn’t as good compared to others who work here – lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, she lost respect mainly from the first lecture, because she came in 10 minutes late and then spent another 10 minutes trying to set up, and was very moody and the lecture hadn’t started so we were talking – I think we were still talking mainly about the last lecture, and she just turned round and shouted at everyone about not being able to hear herself think. As soon as she started the lecture we shut up straight away. She then had another go at the class about finally we were actually able to be quiet, her notes – 52 pages of notes on the first lecture for – it was meant to be for the whole course but there were so many mistakes in it and they were somebody else’s notes she’d edited. So everyone just lost patience with her – completely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And nothing, despite all your efforts, was done about it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you have a personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are they male or female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Male.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you been to them or are they approachable if you needed to go to them?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: They’re approachable erm yeah – Colin’s quite good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you happy with him being a male personal tutor or would you rather have had a female?

turns.speaker: Subject
