turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, who or what do you think has been the greatest influence on you, since you started your degree?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, that’s a big one (it’s OK) I’ve no idea (that’s OK)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You said earlier that you’ve had some problems with group work. (yes) Has the type of teaching that you’ve had involved quite a lot of groupwork?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: There’s 2 or 3 yes, so it’s not too much, but they tend to be things like double modules and things (yeah) – so they count for a lot but it’s a not a lot of actual work in the group.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you work in groups do you get to choose yourself who you work with or are you put into groups?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, half the time you get to choose and half the time you get put in groups. For lab work and things, most of the time we’re given the option, we’ll be put into groups, but if you want someone particularly in the group – if you email them they’ll arrange it, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you decide who to work with in those situations?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, normally I don’t pick who I work with, I just erm wait till everyone else has been put in the group and work with somebody new because I’d rather work with as many people as possible, even if it’s just so that when there is a point where I am put in a group with someone – I know how much I can trust them to get things done. (OK) If we’ve got to pick groups, it’s generally people I’ve worked with before, or people I get on fairly well with.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you had any particular good or bad experiences of working in groups?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, recently we had a meeting for a CAD MAC project. The day before it was due in to finish off, out of 4 of us, only 2 turned up – 1 of them sent an email telling us it was – that the coursework wasn’t due until the week after, so he wasn’t going to meet until next week. Erm, which arrived after getting an email saying that we were definitely handing it in this week. But that’s kind of the worst one so far – well, other than working with my house mate but that’s just a bad idea, it was more my own fault, so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, do you think that men or women are better to work with or is it…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really mixed groups tend to be the best – well I find – well because if there are a couple of guys on the course who – where they’ve actually done – specially design and make projects, where they’ve actually done some machining or things, they tend to try to take over. And if you’ve got a mixed group, usually you can get some back up for everything you’re going to say. Even if it’s just quieting everyone down so they’ll actually listen. Er, it’s also because we do actually look at things a slightly different way, and it just brings up a few more alternatives (yeah) to look at, and things to take into account.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that’s maybe another advantage of having female engineers, that they bring a different perspective?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What aspects of university teaching or advice, do you think will help you on your placement if you go?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know, ‘cos I’ve managed to avoid applying for anything which has to go through the placement officer

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there a particular reason for that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t like the idea of it being put through – that these are [university] students – they are meant to be the best and being put in for companies who always take in [university] students, which seem to be what most of those ones are. I’d rather have sent in my CV, covering letter or do the on-line thing, and just say, this is me, this is what I’ve done, do you want to employ me or not?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So they’re taking you because you are a [university] student. OK, what skills from the course do you think that you’ll take to a placement with you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think a lot of the CAD design work will go with me because up until university I hated doing any design work (yeah) whatsoever and just because of the sheer volume of it, we’ve had to do and things, erm, I’ve got used to it and I kind of know how the process works in industry from things like [company 2] and stuff.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, do you think those work experiences will help you on your placement as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, just ‘cos it gives me an idea of company culture and the way things work – kind of where it comes at this point, this department works and then this department (?) comes to there – we do this and all the rest of it so, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you feel prepared and ready to go on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, mostly. I’m still a bit worried about not knowing enough, especially because I don’t know exactly where I’m going or what I’ll be expected to do at that company.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, what sort of companies have you been applying to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Everything from er [company] to [company], erm [organisation] – anything which sounds like it could be more than just being sat at an office doing one thing time and time again, so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So the criteria that you’ve set when you’re looking for companies have been quite broad?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK do you think that your educational experience, or the way that you’re taught, reflects the realities of what it’ll be like when you’re working in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yes, especially the 2nd year because the 1st year was all – because it was just, you need to learn this (yeah) and now the lecturers are a lot more, well, you just look it up because if you’re working, you just find this handbook and go there and you do it like this and sort of – they aren’t so heavily into things like deriving certain formulas and things – well, you know this, so you can just do this or you’ve made this assumption, you can do that or you don’t need to worry about making it exact. If it passes that then do an exact point, so it’s much more realistic than being sat down and told the exact way you need to do x, y and z.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think the group work will help you in terms of not say the technical skills, but interacting with other people as well? Do you think that bit’s useful?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, just to know what it’s like to be working with new people and different people and even when it does go wrong, how to, kind of deal with it – and get the project done instead of sitting, complaining about it and causing problems.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the placement idea, in general, is a good idea and that students should be encouraged to go on placements?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, because if nothing else, 4 years is a very long time and because you don’t do like engineering A level, or whatever, it is a good time to go and look at the industry and sort of – like, you might turn round and say, well actually no, this isn’t what I need to be doing. And instead of, like wasting another 2 years doing something you really hate and can see like nothing else in the future, you can turn around and try to do something else or think of something new.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you know anyone on your course that isn’t going, or doesn’t want to go on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yeah but most of them are either doing a BEng and kind of have a job waiting for them when they go out or they’ve already taken gap years and don’t want to be, like, 26 when they graduate or whatever, so they just want to sort it out. But then again most of them are planning to go on the graduate development where they do 2 years of more or less a placement before you start work and things like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, has anyone tried to really encourage you or discourage you from going on a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, not really – occasionally you get a few comments about just doing the 4 years to get it finished and then go and earn money, but nothing really serious.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And what about comments from friends and family or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Friends of the family – I think people who are already in electrical engineering or things like that and they don’t see the point – it’s just wasting a year. Its their opinion and their entitled to it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, you said you have applied for the placements off your own back (yeah) have the university supported you doing that…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, a lot of them came off a list we were given. They said these people will take placements, which came off a list. Not a lot of placements on the list were actually, you must apply through the university, so it’s not too bad. I don’t think the university mind as long as you end up somewhere, or decide what you’re doing, because in the long run, it’s your placement, you can go where you want.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: But have the university been supportive, if you do need to go to them for help and (Yeah) in finding stuff. The type of companies that you’ve been applying to - is there anything that particularly attracted you to them or have you been completely open minded, or are you thinking …

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’ve been completely open minded, yeah but I’m most interested in looking at things which look at research rather than design work, or where I can go out on site for a bit and come back, and things like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you, when you’ve been considering organisations, looked at things other than the type of work they do, have you looked at things like training opportunities, and pay and equal opportunities, or anything like that, or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I’ve looked a bit at the training but most companies I’ve looked at er things like the [company], [company], have the training programmes in place and they mention that well, if you do this we might sort of take you on afterwards (yeah), and put you on graduate development, and things like that – which is a bonus but I’m not going to go and apply to someone I’m not particularly keen on so that I can get extra training.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, OK. How long have you got to wait to find out?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, when the companies decide to tell me and we’ve been told that people still advertise placements up to June (oh right) and in some cases people aren’t giving placements until like the October. So I think its generally up to you, when you put a cut off point on when you came to – you turn round and just say well, you’re not getting a placement now, I’d just carry on (yeah) or take a year out – see what happens.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, OK. Did you start off with the list that the University gave you and then where did you do from there? Did you go and look at their web sites?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Go and look at web sites or email them, asking them for material on it and stuff.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And have you had to have any interviews?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, just the one with [company] at the moment.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what type of things are you expecting to get out of your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, just knowing where I want to be heading when I finish here – kind of an idea of how industry works instead of the classroom kind of environment so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Kind of putting the theory into practice (yeah). OK, do you think that it will improve your career prospects at the end being able to say that you have been on a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, ‘cos it shows that you have got some idea of erm being grounded in industry rather than saying I know all this theory like everyone else does. You can apply it, knowing what’s needed for what and…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think could be the worst and the best things about being on a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, the best thing will be meeting – making new contacts (yeah) because a lot of the companies will help you – like find me a project and things and helping you out with information. The worst is probably moving to wherever the placement is and being somewhere completely new and having to live with total strangers (yeah) for a whole year where you can’t just turn round and then say no, I’m not going to have this any more.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you applied to organisations over quite a wide geography then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. What are you most looking forward to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, being back in the real world – if that doesn’t sound really strange but [university town] is just [university town] because there’s so many students here, I don’t really hear the outside world too much, it’s [this university’s] done this, or [this university’s] done that – it’s just being out there and being, you know, being normal again – going to work, earning money, working regular time and going out and doing what you want at the weekends and coming back.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What type of work do you hope to be doing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Research, hopefully.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: And defence would be an ideal but erm such high standards are required for it, I’d be lucky to get in there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how do you expect work to differ from university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, much more scheduled and much more your own responsibility and therefore, you need to plan for this week and this for next week – being given an end point to aim for and to do it yourself – just being able to do 9 till 5 and then anything else is what you want to do – what you need to do because you haven’t done it during your day role, and random hours and having to fill most of them, if you haven’t quite sorted yourself out.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And are you looking forward to that side of it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, er much more structured routine would just be nice for a change – instead of random hours, just knowing what’s happening.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, in terms of your career, where do you see yourself in 2 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In 2 years time, erm, I’ll be in my 3rd – just to finish my 3rd year and to go into my 4th year – (?) I won’t really be…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Alright, what about in 5 years?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, hopefully, I’ll have just finished the graduate development programme – somewhere – and be looking at erm getting myself in whatever area I’ve found useful during the programme (uh huh) and starting work for real.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, what about in 10 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hopefully I will have got my chartership (yeah) and still working for the same company – possibly.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what would be your ideal career?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, my ideal would be working for someone like [company] on [place] because they have the funding, with being linked to the MoD and there erm defence, but when they became a public company did a lot more alternative work as well now – freelance work – so you wouldn’t ever be – you’d still have the main defence work which has a huge amount of innovation, most of the time, but you’d still be able to come out of that and still do something much more down to earth or new and interesting. It’s just – split it up so I didn’t I end up being one of these people like er at [company 2], where they just know everything about the one product, but if you try and talk to them about something else, it always comes back to focussing on the stair lift and it becomes very closed as to how you look at things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that you will come across many difficulties trying to get that ideal career? Do you think it’s realistic?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it’s possible erm, they’re still trying to recruit a lot more people at the moment. As long as my grades stay up, I’m in for a chance – everyone’s in for a chance.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, so the main thing between you and that, you think is, academic?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Is grades, if I can. Well Kinetic is – it’s kind of local to where I’m from – it’s where the – if you had someone from engineering come into schools – it’d be someone who’s from the MoD, and then it became Kinetic and things like that, so I’ve always had a link with them. (Yeah) So, I think if I can get the grades, I want to work there to the point where, hopefully, if I manage to get to an interview, I’ll be able to put it across that even if I’m borderline on academics and experience, I’ve got enough enthusiasm and determination to want to work with them – that it’ll be enough to get me the job.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you applied to them for a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No because they’ve stopped doing placements this year. They’ve started doing sponsorship programme instead (OK) which you can’t apply to once you’re at university.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, and would you have been interested in doing the sponsorship at the time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I was, but I didn’t see companies I knew much about and I was a bit dubious about signing up for, and taking money off them to be doing a summer placement every year – a year out with them and turning out that actually, no ...

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, what if you didn’t actually want it …

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: If [company] had been offering one then I’d have probably gone for it (yeah) because I knew about them, same for a couple of others, but at the time it didn’t seem applicable.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that career prospects are good in your field of engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, because they can’t – the quotas at the moment, for graduates in mechanical engineering aren’t that good, they’re just trying to get more people in and it’s – on my course a lot of the people who are there are on – didn’t apply for mechanical engineering, they’re people who tried for auto or aero and didn’t make the grades, and considering some of the grades required, if you wanted to get onto the course – first time – the fact that there’s still loads of clearing places and they’re able to put as many people on there as wanted, just shows that they really do need to have a lot more graduates with a degree, than we’re getting.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about the prospects once you’re inside a company for going into say the managing side of it, would you be interested in doing that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I would prefer to stay with research but a lot of people I’ve talked to in companies, its more or less, if you have a degree, you can get almost straight into managerial positions if you want to but I personally find – hold off doing that until I’ve had at least 2/3 years working almost at ground level and learning that – ‘cos I don’t think it’s right to go – to manage a thing when you have no idea about how it works and when you’ve only just got into grips with the company and things like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. And are you happy with the career choices that you’ve made so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you do anything differently if you had to do it all again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yes, possibly talk to a few more people who had done engineering, just to make myself slightly more aware of the workload and what to expect. (yeah) But, apart from that, no.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how would you describe the culture or the characteristics of the engineering industry in 5 words?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, rooted in old ways (traditional) yeah, you can see the same kind of patterns everywhere, it doesn’t change much even when new productions methods or new things – it kind of alters a little bit and then it goes back into the same old patterns. Its well established – it doesn’t – it takes quite a bit to do a shake up, completely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that’s maybe the reason why there don’t seem to be more women going into engineering – whereas they maybe doing in other fields?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, possibly. I think it’s more this image of the boiler suits and things and then looking at sort of the money and things, because for the same A level courses, if you did computing - I mean its even obvious with my house mate who’s doing a placement next year in computing – she’s getting 17 ½ grand for her placement year (blimey) – whereas I’m looking at 12. So it’s kind of looking at career choices and first impressions of it, because if you don’t think you’re going to be doing as well, you won’t look into it further to see sort of what you can do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the engineering culture is masculine?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, fairly but just because it always has been and how it started off, was very much sort of, most companies was a guy who built something and then it became a company so everyone – and a lot of people – the companies I’ve worked in, have started off doing things, like apprenticeships rather than degrees, so they have worked on the shop floor, and they do know everything about it and they can like strip down whatever they’re building and build it back up in like 2 seconds. And I’ve been to some companies – 30 years they’ve been going – as an under grad going, I’d do it like this, and they’re like, well no, and they can just see everything – and it does give you the perception that everything is really hands-on (yeah) whereas you stay there for a few weeks and you actually realise that no, they haven’t done that in like 30 years – so, it’s just the way they’ve started bringing people in.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that if more women do go into the industry, that will break those perceptions down?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it’ll start to, especially as they start getting higher up, because then they’ll be like role models. It’s like engineering – you’ve got [university] and people like that, and its like, the guy who did railways and bridges and big heavy things like – they’re either like – the only vaguely engineering woman, I think she’s – I can’t think of her name – she’s a materials engineer and she’s done a lot of work on polymers and stuff, so she’s a Royal Fellow now, but that’s the only the one I’ve heard of and that’s only because I read things like New Scientist and that lot, so haven’t kind of been pointed to, oh look this woman managed to do it and all the rest of it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that role models are important then (yeah) to encourage people?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well with big role models, because – I mean, with WES here, it’s like they occasionally get someone in to talk and it’s like, oh she is a manager of a project for – oh it’s sort of, yes, she has a job, she has the same kind of managerial role as anyone else who’d have it and it’s not really that inspiring – like you’ll end up in that job rather than you’d be famous for it, you know, and it’s like, computers have their people to look at and sort of biologists and engineering is just kind of a few big men at the top and you don’t know much else at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think any aspects of the engineering culture will be problematic for you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really but then again I work with people – when I worked for [company 2] and things they were really accommodating about it, and they were very aware of the fact that they need a lot more women. A lot of them were much more receptive to we need more people and if it comes in the form of women – we don’t care. We just need to get the fresh in-takes coming in, so I don’t think it’ll be too big a problem. It’ll just be maybe, some people who’ve been there a long time and aren’t used to it, being a bit strange, but I mean that’s getting used to anything. You could say if you suddenly gave me a new computer system, they’d be a bit odd. But I don’t think it’s anything that’s like directly related to suddenly having a woman in the workplace.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think your educational experience is different from other students, say in social sciences?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I don’t know – more because – because of the A levels I did, I’ve always been associated with people who’ve done similar courses so I don’t really know enough people who’ve done – the none sciences – to gauge if it’s that much different, if you know what I mean.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, you mentioned WES, have you been in that group since you started university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’ve been a member since I was 16 (right) with outside groups and doing their insight course. Last year I was a member here and was part of one their projects. Technically, I’m a member now but I haven’t been involved in it, after last year because it was - I couldn’t see much reason for some of the things they were doing (right, OK) so it didn’t seem like it was worth it when I could be concentrating on other things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What sorts of things were they involved in?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well a lot of it is getting women in from the industry as – like a role model, like a [company] production line manager which, having someone talk about their job as a production line manager, especially having worked for a bit in production, with [company 2], I’d much rather go out and try and get myself experience – you’re writing to companies – than to be sitting, having someone telling me I’ve become a Chartered Engineer, it’s great, you can do it too, because if I didn’t think I could do it, I wouldn’t be here – yeah, and there’s just – they run other projects, which sound really worthwhile trying to get kids into engineering, especially girls, erm last year it was an email mentoring but people they’re targeting aren’t organised enough for it to work. I ended up mentoring a girl who just didn’t do any emails – didn’t want to know. She’d been put in there because the school said she was in the A set at maths, therefore she should want to do things like engineering. She didn’t. She wanted to be a biologist, which I know nothing about, so even if she had emailed me about what she wanted to do, I couldn’t have helped her. It’s just badly organised. I mean some things this year, are things like lego competition, which is a national thing and they were just helping out with – are really good causes and I’d love to do it but I don’t have the time to do it and I don’t have the inclination to take out the 3 hours.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think there’s anything different that they should be doing that they’re maybe not doing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think because this is a student group erm it’s being more aimed at trying to get people into the uni, than getting people outside to do better, or to get companies who already work with the uni to go oh, we’re great. Erm, ‘cos a lot of the other groups are doing things like we’ve managed to get a trip to so and so’s factory. They’re going to give us a tour, show us how it all works, so if you’re interested come to that. They’re running conferences in the centres and things, which sounds really interesting if I could get – but they’re not accessible from here.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, do you think that the mentoring idea is a good idea in general? Not just say you being a mentor, but would you like to have a mentor as you went into the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah – I mean at A level, we had various mentors and things and it’s always just given me someone to bounce off ideas with or to just check that even if it’s like, just a random person, but it’s one of these things I think you’ve got to want to do and your mentor’s got to want to do because if you can’t be bothered or just don’t want to know, you know, and then you don’t want to do it and it’s just like oh, I won’t bother then. As long as both people involved are active for it – up for it, I think it’s a great scheme, but it’s a case of choosing who’s involved with what.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that’s everything thank you very much.
